Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy. At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening.2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings.

If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does. Let me turn to the economy. [OFFICIAL] output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout.

I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace. The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance.

While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated.

If hires and separations are low because worker matches have improved, then this may be a boost to productivity and can be largely ignored in assessing the state of the labor market. But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth. This possibility is important to monitor because productivity growth is a crucial factor in judging how fast the economy can grow without undesirable inflationary pressure. As I said earlier, I don't have the answers to the questions I have posed, but I believe the questions are worth asking and addressing with more research.

Let me put aside this discussion about the health of the labor market for now. What is important in the near term is that I see the labor market as stable and employment at a level close to the FOMC's maximum-employment goal. By contrast, inflation is well above 2 percent and the focus of my attention. For reasons I explained at the start of this speech, I was willing to wait to tighten monetary policy at the FOMC's October meeting. Inconveniently for today's event, we will get consumer price index (CPI) inflation for October in a few hours. While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting.

However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for. Let's just say it. September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining. Inflation based on personal consumption expenditures (PCE), the measure targeted by the FOMC, rose at a monthly rate of 0.5 percent in September and 3.7 percent over the previous 12 months. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September and 3.1 percent from that time last year. Both these measures are too high, and I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases. Earlier this year, excessive inflation was driven by nonmarket prices that are estimated rather than observed by the government, and ones that I tend to discount as hard to measure and as an unreliable guide to the overall trend for core inflation.

But now, two components with greater relevance to future inflation are elevated—core goods prices and those for core market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of the components of core PCE service prices saw 12-month increases above 3 percent in September. Later today, I will be looking to see whether this breadth of elevated inflation continues, including whether high-tech goods prices related to the AI buildout continue to rise at the very high rate of recent months. I also want to know if the run-up in energy prices of the past several months is being passed through to goods and services directly or indirectly, because of higher input costs. While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained.

Federal Reserve staff have been thinking hard about the effects on inflation of the AI buildout and elevated energy prices, and their findings do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon. In one exercise, researchers tried to capture imminent price pressures with a textual analysis of the well-known surveys of purchasing managers conducted by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM).5 ISM surveys ask purchasing managers to list specific commodities, materials, and services whose prices rose or fell that month.6 Staff used these responses to construct monthly price pressure indexes that correspond with actual categories of the producer price index (PPI). They found these indexes provide information about future changes in producer prices and, as a result, should have some signal about future PCE inflation.

For example, the index for high-tech products rose in December 2025 and jumped further in January 2026, ahead of an escalation in those goods prices that eventually showed up in the February PPI and inflation data. The most recent ISM data, for October, point to the possibility of more price increases ahead. Some other Fed research indicates to me that energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past.7 The researchers find a potential shift in the inflation process after the pandemic that suggests core inflation may be more responsive to energy shocks. Central bankers have tended to look through energy price shocks and expect that their effects on inflation will soon fade, but this new work cautions against taking too much comfort in this view.

To recap my economic outlook, economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC's 2 percent goal. This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting. That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting.

Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.
